newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian debt markets - Dah Sing securitises home loans.
newsitem.headline: Asian debt markets - Dah Sing securitises home loans.

text.p: Dah Sing Bank plans a US$300 million cross-border credit-enhanced mortgage securitisation due out next week, it announced on Thursday.
Executives at the bank said it was the biggest cross-border mortgage or asset-backed deal originated in Asia, excluding Japan. Launch date should be on or about June 18.
It is the latest in a series of mortgage securitisations -- Hong Kong Telecommunications Co Ltd and the Hong Kong arm of Sanwa Bank have both securitised mortgages recently.
The deal is seen as demonstrating growing investor appetite for such issues and growing need by mortgage lenders to clear loans from their balance sheets.
Interestingly, the notes will be listed in Luxembourg, but will not be offered to U.S. investors.

Bank of China is to raise US$200 million through a five-year floating-rate note arranged by Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp, Daiwa Securities' Hong Kong branch, and Bank of China International, bankers said.
No pricing has emerged, but it is tipped to be considering offering an all-in yield in the low 30s, possibly 32-33 basis points, according to one European banker.
If true, this was seen as reasonable, considering China Construction bank's five-year FRN is trading at about 30 basis points in the secondary market at about 30 basis points.
Bankers also said Agriculture Bank of China (ABC) is expected to launch a US$120 million five-year floating-rate certificate of deposit (FRCD) through its Singapore branch.
ABC has yet to gain regulatory approval in China and no mandate has been awarded yet.
Bankers said Guangdong Development Bank may tap the capital market again, having just completed a US$50 million three-year FRCD through its Macau branch.
Chinese toll road operator Greater Beijing Region Expressways Ltd is expected to launch its US$275 million Yankee imminently, traders said.
The Yankee bond is a 144a transaction and is in two tranches -- one for seven years and one for 10 years.
Morgan Stanley is lead managing the issue.
Unconfirmed pricing talk suggests the seven-year tranche will be launched at 200 basis points above the U.S. treasuries for the seven-year tranche.
Chase Manhattan opted for bond-style syndication in Hong Kong with a deal priced in line with recent deals from major banks in the territory.
"I think the deal will most probably fly," said the managing director of a European bank.
Chase launched its HK$2 billion floating-rate certificate of deposit issue at par, priced to float at 20 basis points over the One-Month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR).
This was identical to Standard Chartered Bank's pricing on its FRCD May last week, and two basis points below that of Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corp's FRCD issue in May.
A Japanese banker said the price was all right, given the Aa2 long-term rating of Chase's parent, although this issue was expected to attract an A1 rating.
Chase Manhattan plans to seek eligibility for the liquidity adjustment facility operated by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.
